title: Young Exiles in a Foreign Palace
overview: After Babylon conquers Jerusalem, Daniel and three friends are trained to serve its king, and they find a way to stay loyal to their God while succeeding in a foreign court.

parts.label: Jerusalem falls to Babylon (vv. 1-2)
parts.note: Babylon's king besieged Jerusalem, and the writer says the Lord handed Judah's king over to him, along with some sacred objects from God's temple. The Babylonian king put those objects in his own god's temple treasury, a common way for conquerors to give their god credit for the victory, while the writer presents it as the Lord's doing.

parts.label: Captives trained for the palace (vv. 3-5)
parts.note: The king then ordered gifted young men from Judah's royal and noble families to be brought in and schooled for three years in Babylon's language and learning, eating from the king's own table. Empires often trained a conquered people's young elite this way, to turn them into capable and loyal officials.

parts.label: New names, new identity (vv. 6-7)
parts.note: The four friends' Hebrew names all honor Israel's God; Daniel, for example, means "God is my judge." Their new Babylonian names seem to point to Babylon's gods instead, marking them as the king's men, though scholars are unsure of the exact meaning of each.

parts.label: Daniel refuses the king's food (vv. 8-14)
parts.note: Daniel decided the royal food and wine would make him unclean before God, though the text does not explain exactly why. He asked politely rather than defying anyone, and when the official feared for his own life, Daniel proposed a ten day trial of vegetables and water.

parts.label: The test and the result (vv. 15-20)
parts.note: The four looked healthier than the others, and the writer credits God with giving them unusual learning, and Daniel the ability to understand dreams and visions. When the king examined them, he found them far wiser than all his own advisers, which sets up the stories that follow.

parts.label: Daniel lasts through the exile (v. 21)
parts.note: Cyrus of Persia took Babylon in 539 BC and soon let exiles return home. So Daniel, one of the first captives taken, lived to see the end of the exile, and a later chapter shows him still alive after that.

disagreement: Readers differ on why Daniel drew the line at the king's food, whether because of Jewish food laws, food first offered to idols, or refusing to depend wholly on the king, and so on what kind of faithfulness the story is holding up.
think: When you have had to fit into a culture or system that was not your own, what did you go along with, and what did you quietly hold on to?
